methodology.title: How this works
methodology.subtitle: The signals behind your score, in plain English.
methodology.overallP: Each signal — publisher reputation, article quality, tone & balance, and (when Deep Analysis runs) fact-check evidence — is turned into a likelihood ratio and combined additively in log-odds space. The final number is the probability of credibility that falls out of that combination. Because signals multiply rather than average, strong evidence (a high-tier publisher, a matching fact-check) pulls the score meaningfully; a contradicting fact-check can now drop the score further than the old weighted-sum ever allowed. Alongside the point score we compute a 95% credible interval from a Beta posterior: a narrow band means the signals converge and we're confident, a wide band means we're honestly less sure.
methodology.publisherP: Pulled from our curated list (~50 publishers, hand-picked from Wikipedia's Perennial Sources editor consensus plus a Chinese-language publisher set) plus the IFCN signatory list of certified fact-checkers. If we don't recognize the publisher, we fall back to article-level signals (HTTPS, byline present, article length, extracted publisher name). Fallback scores are bounded 30–60 and the rating strength indicator drops to "low".
methodology.qualityH: Article quality + tone & balance + devil's advocate
methodology.qualityP: All three come from a single call to Claude (an AI model from Anthropic). The model reads the article and returns: a 0–100 quality score, a –5 to +5 tone & balance estimate (LLM-estimated, low rating strength on its own), and the strongest argument that the rating could be wrong. The devil's advocate is always shown because it trains media literacy.
methodology.deepP: The "Run Deep Analysis" button on a result spawns three more Claude calls in sequence: a SKEPTIC searching for every reason to distrust the article, an ADVOCATE searching for every reason to trust it, and a JUDGE weighing both reports and returning a final verdict. Each agent cites specific evidence from the article. Costs ~3-5× a normal check and takes ~10-20s.
methodology.deepP2: KNOWN LIMITATION: in V1 all three agents are the same model family (Claude), so they share underlying biases. A future update will mix model families for genuine bias reduction.
methodology.factCheckH: How we fact-check claims (Deep Analysis only)
methodology.factCheckP1: During Deep Analysis we also run a five-stage fact-check pipeline:
methodology.factCheckP2:
1. An LLM extracts up to 3 verifiable factual claims from the article (numbers, named events, quotes — not opinions).
2. We query the Google Fact Check Tools API, which aggregates fact-checks from PolitiFact, Snopes, AFP Fact Check, Reuters Fact Check, and dozens of other IFCN-signatory outlets.
3. We search the open web via Brave Search and keep only results from a hand-curated list of ~30 Tier-1 publishers (Reuters, AP, BBC, NYT, etc.) — everything else is discarded.
4. Named entities (people, organizations, events) are checked against Wikipedia to catch fabricated names. Chinese-locale checks hit zh.wikipedia.org first, then fall back to English.
5. A second LLM call synthesizes all the evidence into a per-claim verdict (corroborated / contradicted / no fact-checks found / mixed) and adjusts the article's overall score by up to ±30 points.
methodology.ratingP:
Falls out of the width of the 95% credible interval:
• High — narrow band (≤15 points). Signals converge.
• Medium — mid band (16–30 points).
• Low — wide band (>30 points). Typical for unknown publishers or when signals disagree.
Computed from the per-signal precision weights, not LLM judgment, so it's consistent across calls.
methodology.todoP: No real bias dataset (we use an LLM estimate today), no domain-age lookup. Our Tier-1 publisher allowlist is hand-curated and skews US/UK, with a Chinese-language set added for diaspora users. Coverage in other languages and regions is the next focus area.
methodology.feedbackP: Every result has Helpful / Not helpful buttons. Not helpful opens a short comment box. Your feedback shapes future improvements to the scoring and explanations.
methodology.legalNote: Both open in Safari. Hosted publicly so they can be updated without an app release.

limitations.title: Limitations
limitations.subtitle: What Debunkr does — and what it can't.
limitations.b1: AI analysis. Output may contain errors. Treat as a starting point, not a verdict.
limitations.b2: Paywalled or JavaScript-only articles often can not be read by the backend. Rating strength drops or the check fails.
limitations.b3: Breaking news. A single article in isolation is hard to judge; cross-reference matters.
limitations.b4: Satire. We do not yet detect satire — sites like The Onion may be rated as low credibility.
limitations.b5: Opinion vs reporting. The score evaluates writing quality, not whether you should agree with the opinion.
limitations.b6: Publisher reputation is curated (~50 publishers from Wikipedia's Perennial Sources list, a Chinese-language publisher set, and IFCN-signatory fact-checkers). Coverage will expand over time.
limitations.b7: Tone & balance is an LLM estimate, not a real bias dataset (AllSides license still pending). Treat it with caution.
limitations.b8: URLs you check are temporarily cached server-side (max 24 hours) so repeat checks of the same article respond faster. We don't sell or share them. See the Privacy Policy for the full data flow.
limitations.b9: Fact-check coverage is strongest in English. Chinese-language fact-check APIs are limited — we surface AFP / Reuters Chinese-language pieces where available.
limitations.b10: Breaking news (less than 24 hours old) often has no fact-check or Tier-1 coverage yet. We will say "no fact-checks found" rather than guess.
limitations.b11: Fabricated entities slip through if they are not yet on Wikipedia — and some real people aren't on Wikipedia either, so this is not perfect.
limitations.b12: Our Tier-1 publisher list is hand-picked and skews US/UK/HK English-language plus a Chinese-language set. Quality sources in other regions may not be reflected.
limitations.b13: The aggregator LLM can hallucinate citations. We cap citation count at 5 and require URLs come from the actual search results, but errors are still possible.

mediaLit.title: Media literacy
mediaLit.subtitle: Skills for spotting bad info — not just our rating.
mediaLit.siftIntro: Four moves you can run on any article in under a minute. Build the habit and you'll catch most misinformation before it sticks.
mediaLit.siftFootnote: SIFT is the most-evidenced media-literacy framework, developed by Mike Caulfield. Used widely in journalism schools.
mediaLit.tacticsIntro: Once you know these, you'll see them everywhere.
mediaLit.disclaimer: Debunkr is a tool for media literacy practice — it doesn't replace your own judgment. The skills above work even when our score is wrong.

sift.stopBody: When a story makes you feel strong emotion, pause. Strong emotion is the most common trigger for sharing misinformation. Don't engage until you've checked.
sift.investigateBody: Open a new tab. Search '[publisher name] Wikipedia' or '[publisher name] reliability'. Don't rely only on the site's About page.
sift.findBody: Search the same story across multiple sources. If only one publisher is reporting a major event, that's a red flag. If reliable sources contradict it, trust them.
sift.traceBody: Most news articles are about something — a study, a statement, an event. Find the primary source. Quotes can be cropped. Statistics can be misrepresented. Go upstream when you can.

tactics.loadedBody: Words that smuggle in opinion. 'Bombshell report' vs 'investigation finds'. Read the same story in two outlets and compare the verbs.
tactics.falseEqBody: Treating a major scandal and a minor mistake as 'both sides did something wrong'. Look for where the article downplays a significant difference.
tactics.cherryBody: Picking the one statistic that supports the argument while ignoring the rest. Ask: was this the only data point available? What was the trend over time?
tactics.anonBody: Sometimes necessary (whistleblowers). Often a red flag (no accountability). The most reliable articles cite named people you can verify.
tactics.imageTitle: Image and video out of context
tactics.imageBody: A real photo from a different event. A real quote cropped to remove qualifiers. Reverse-image-search and check timestamps.
tactics.headlineBody: Many readers share based on headline alone. The headline often overpromises what the article actually proves. Read the body, especially the middle.

OVERALL CREDIBILITY.whatThisChecks: A combined score: 45% publisher reputation, 45% AI-judged article quality, 10% tone & balance.
OVERALL CREDIBILITY.askYourself: Does the score match your gut read? A weak score from a strong source — or vice versa — is worth a closer look.

RATING STRENGTH.whatThisChecks: How much data we had to make this rating. High = we knew the publisher and read the article cleanly. Low = we had to fall back to article-level signals.
RATING STRENGTH.askYourself: When rating strength is low, treat the score as a guess, not a verdict. Look for primary sources yourself.

ARTICLE.whatThisChecks: The title, author, and a short excerpt extracted from the page.
ARTICLE.askYourself: Does the headline match what the article actually says? Is there a named author with verifiable credentials?

BREAKDOWN.whatThisChecks: The three signals that produced the overall score, scored independently.
BREAKDOWN.askYourself: If one signal is much lower than the others, that's where to focus your skepticism.

PUBLISHER.whatThisChecks: Who published this and how reputable they are by independent assessment (Wikipedia Perennial Sources, IFCN).
PUBLISHER.askYourself: Even reputable publishers can be wrong. Even unknown publishers can be correct. Reputation is one signal, not the truth.

DEVIL'S ADVOCATE.whatThisChecks: An AI-generated argument for why the rating could be wrong. We always show this.
DEVIL'S ADVOCATE.askYourself: Read this BEFORE deciding. The strongest version of the opposite view trains your media literacy more than agreeing with the score.

DEEP ANALYSIS.whatThisChecks: Three sequential AI calls (Skeptic, Advocate, Judge) plus an external fact-check pipeline against Google Fact Check Tools and Wikipedia.
DEEP ANALYSIS.askYourself: Read the Skeptic and Advocate sections before the Judge. Watch where they disagree.

didKnowTips.t0: When a story makes you feel strong emotion, pause before sharing. Strong emotion is the #1 driver of misinformation spread.
didKnowTips.t1: Lateral reading — opening new tabs to verify — is faster AND more accurate than carefully evaluating one source.
didKnowTips.t2: Anonymous sources are sometimes necessary (whistleblowers), often a red flag. The most reliable articles cite named, verifiable people.
didKnowTips.t3: A headline can be misleading even when the article is accurate. Always read past the headline before sharing.
didKnowTips.t4: Real photos used in fake contexts is the most common form of visual misinformation. A reverse image search takes 10 seconds.
didKnowTips.t5: If only one publisher is reporting a major event, that's a red flag. Mainstream stories get covered by multiple Tier-1 sources.
